VBO:0000661.summary: Broholmers tend to be calm, friendly and quietly watchful, combining a companion’s affection with a guardian’s self-confidence. Their Danish ancestors moved from stag hunting to watching over farms and manor houses. After the breed nearly disappeared following World War II, enthusiasts began rebuilding its population in the 1970s.
VBO:0000661.interestingFact: The name comes from Broholm, the estate associated with Sehested’s early work to establish the breed.
VBO:0000661.historicalRoots: Danish estate and guard dog; modern revival began in the 1970s.

sources.title: FCI: Broholmer breed standard
sources.evidence: Calm, friendly, watchful, self-confident temperament; stag hunting followed by estate guarding; near extinction after WWII and revival around 1975; Broholm name.

VBO:0200088.summary: Australian Cattle Dogs are intensely alert, devoted workers with a strong protective streak; they can be wary of unfamiliar people. Their task was to gather and move cattle across unfenced Australian country, where persistence and the ability to keep working over long distances mattered. That focus on a job remains central to the breed’s character.
VBO:0200088.historicalRoots: Developed in Australia for long-distance cattle work.

sources.title: FCI: Australian Cattle Dog breed standard
sources.evidence: Watchful intelligence, devotion to duty, protective instincts and suspicion of strangers; developed to muster and move wild cattle with stamina on unfenced properties.

VBO:0200108.summary: Azawakhs often reserve their affection for a trusted circle, showing a gentle side with familiar people while keeping their distance from strangers. They share camp life with pastoral communities of the Sahel, where their work has included pursuing game and defending against predators. Attentiveness and close family bonds are as much a part of their story as speed.
VBO:0200108.interestingFact: In the Tuareg language, the Azawakh is known as Oska.
VBO:0200108.historicalRoots: Sahelian sighthound associated with pastoral communities of Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso.

sources.title: FCI: Azawakh breed standard
sources.evidence: Reserved with strangers, gentle and affectionate with accepted people; camp companionship, game pursuit and predator defense; Tuareg name Oska.

VBO:0200120.summary: Basenjis tend to be independent, affectionate and keenly alert, with a reserved approach to strangers and unusually fastidious habits. These Central African hunting companions are famous for communicating without a conventional bark: their repertoire includes a chortling, rising yodel. “Barkless” certainly does not mean voiceless.
VBO:0200120.historicalRoots: Central African hunting dog with long-established regional roots.

sources.title: FCI: Basenji breed standard
sources.evidence: Independent, affectionate, alert, sometimes aloof; notable cleanliness; hunting/companion use and characteristic chortle-yodel rather than bark.

VBO:0200185.summary: Boerboels are confident, devoted guardians with a strong protective instinct and a character that combines watchfulness with composure. Their roots lie in South African homesteads, where dogs guarded the people and property around them. They are also attentive learners, a side of the breed that can be easy to overlook beside its formidable reputation.
VBO:0200185.historicalRoots: South African farm and homestead dog developed from large guardian types.

sources.title: SABBS: Boerboel breed standard, character section
sources.evidence: SABBS character section describes self-confidence, calmness, family loyalty, protective instincts and trainability.

sources.title: AKC: Boerboel working history and character
sources.evidence: AKC describes remote South African homestead guarding, confidence and eagerness to learn.

VBO:0200231.summary: Brazilian Terriers are lively, energetic workers who tend to be warm with familiar people and more suspicious of newcomers. Their background combines small-game hunting, keeping watch and companionship. The breed developed on Brazilian farms from imported terriers and local dogs, then followed farming families into the growing cities.
VBO:0200231.historicalRoots: Brazilian farm terrier shaped by imported terriers and local selection.

sources.title: FCI: Brazilian Terrier breed standard
sources.evidence: Active, keen, alert, friendly with friends and suspicious of strangers; small-game hunting, guarding and companion use; development on farms and movement into cities.

VBO:0200338.summary: Chihuahuas tend to be alert, lively and remarkably self-assured, with the bold, self-reliant character often associated with terriers. Companionship is their central role. The breed takes its name from the Mexican state of Chihuahua; its often-told connection to the older Techichi dogs of Mexico remains a proposed ancestry, not a settled family tree.
VBO:0200338.historicalRoots: Mexican companion breed with debated links to pre-Columbian small dogs.

sources.title: FCI: Chihuahua breed standard
sources.evidence: FCI describes quick, alert, lively, courageous companion character; names Chihuahua state and presents Techichi ancestry as an assumption.

sources.title: AKC: breed temperament guide, Chihuahua
sources.evidence: Chihuahua entry identifies alert temperament with terrier-like confidence and self-reliance.

VBO:0200345.summary: Chinese Cresteds are affectionate, playful companions with an alert interest in what is happening around them. Many enjoy perching on a chair arm or the back of a sofa, a habit that has earned them comparisons with cats. Their eagerness to engage with people also finds an outlet in agility, where trained Cresteds tackle jumps and obstacles with enthusiasm.
VBO:0200345.interestingFact: The entertainer Gypsy Rose Lee maintained an influential Chinese Crested breeding program.
VBO:0200345.historicalRoots: Long-established hairless companion type developed under British patronage from dogs associated with China.

sources.title: FCI: Chinese Crested breed standard
sources.evidence: FCI identifies happy companion temperament; not used to substantiate disputed ancient origin stories.

sources.title: AKC: Chinese Crested breed standard
sources.evidence: AKC Chinese Crested standard describes a loving, playful, entertaining companion and alert temperament.

sources.title: AKC: Chinese Crested habits and history
sources.evidence: Breed article documents high-perching habits, agility and eagerness to please, plus Gypsy Rose Lee’s influential breeding program.

VBO:0200389.summary: Cotons de Tulear are cheerful, sociable companions who tend to enjoy the company of both people and other dogs. Their adaptable, even-tempered character is central to the breed’s identity. From Madagascar, they became established companions in France before spreading more widely.
VBO:0200389.historicalRoots: Companion breed associated with Madagascar and the port of Tulear/Toliara.

sources.title: FCI: Coton de Tulear breed standard
sources.evidence: Happy, stable, sociable with humans and other dogs, adaptable temperament; companion role; Madagascar origin and early establishment in France before wider spread.

VBO:0200406.summary: Dachshunds combine a friendly, even-tempered side with the persistence of a serious hunter. They follow scent with determination, and their traditional work extends well beyond going underground: they also flush game, follow a trail while calling, and track wounded animals above ground. The familiar household companion still carries a remarkably varied hunting résumé.
VBO:0200406.historicalRoots: German hunting dog developed for work below ground.

sources.title: FCI: Dachshund breed standard
sources.evidence: Friendly, even temperament and passionate persistent hunting; underground work plus above-ground flushing, hunting while giving tongue and wounded-game tracking.

VBO:0200526.summary: Finnish Spitz are lively, determined hunters with an independent streak; they can be reserved when meeting strangers. Their distinctive skill is locating game birds in trees and marking the spot by barking, working at a distance while keeping the hunter informed. That purposeful use of their voice is woven into the breed’s character and working tradition.
VBO:0200526.interestingFact: Finland named the Finnish Spitz its national dog in 1979.
VBO:0200526.historicalRoots: Finnish spitz-type hunting dog used to indicate game birds in trees.

sources.title: FCI: Finnish Spitz breed standard
sources.evidence: Independent but cooperative hunting, game marked by barking, lively and determined character with stranger reserve; national dog in 1979.

VBO:0200610.summary: Golden Retrievers tend to be friendly, confident and eager to cooperate, with a strong interest in working alongside people. Their retrieving background calls for finding game and bringing it back over land or water. The breed’s Scottish beginnings are unusually well documented in the Guisachan estate records, where practical working ability and a pleasant character helped shape the dogs.
VBO:0200610.interestingFact: An 1868 mating between Nous and the Tweed Water Spaniel Belle produced the four puppies at the center of the Golden Retriever’s recorded beginnings.
VBO:0200610.historicalRoots: Nineteenth-century Scottish retriever developed for land-and-water gundog work.

sources.title: FCI: Golden Retriever breed standard
sources.evidence: FCI describes biddable, intelligent, naturally capable working character; friendly, kind and confident temperament; gundog role.

sources.title: Golden Retriever Club of America: early ancestors
sources.evidence: GRCA history documents water retrieving heritage, character and usability, Scottish Guisachan records and the four puppies from Nous/Belle’s 1868 litter.

VBO:0200623.summary: Great Danes tend to be affectionate and closely attached to their people, while sometimes taking a more reserved approach to strangers. Their modern companion role follows a history of boar hunting and guarding. Despite the English name, the breed was developed in Germany, where it is known as the Deutsche Dogge.
VBO:0200623.historicalRoots: German giant dog descended from large hunting and estate types.

sources.title: FCI: Great Dane breed standard
sources.evidence: Friendly, loving and devoted to owners, possible reserve toward strangers; companion/watch/guard use; boar-hound ancestry and German development/name.

VBO:0200670.summary: Himalayan Sheepdogs have long worked alongside shepherds, protecting livestock in demanding mountain country. The wider regional group includes dogs maintained by different pastoral communities. Among them, Gaddi dogs accompany sheep and goat herders between high summer pastures and lower winter grazing, making the annual journey as working members of the camp.

sources.title: Frontiers: Gaddi dogs and Himalayan pastoral work
sources.evidence: Study introduction identifies the Himalayan sheepdog group and its livestock protection role; Gaddi community sheep/goat husbandry and seasonal high-pasture/lower-elevation migrations. Specific migration claims are scoped to Gaddi dogs, not every regional population.

VBO:0200744.summary: Jindos are alert, deliberate dogs known for strong attachment to familiar people and a pronounced hunting instinct. They also have a notable sense of direction and tend to keep themselves clean. Their history is rooted on Korea’s Jindo Island, where difficult transport links helped preserve the local dogs over generations.
VBO:0200744.historicalRoots: Korean island spitz associated with Jindo County.

sources.title: FCI: Jindo breed standard
sources.evidence: Strong hunting instinct, careful alert character, attachment to owner, sense of direction and cleanliness; island isolation and difficult transport preserving local type.

VBO:0200800.summary: Labrador Retrievers tend to be outgoing, cooperative and strongly motivated to work with people. A keen nose, enthusiasm for water and a gentle carrying grip are central to their retrieving skills. Their story links working dogs on the Newfoundland coast with British gundog development, where retrieving trials helped establish the breed’s reputation.
VBO:0200800.historicalRoots: Newfoundland water-dog roots; developed as a retriever in Great Britain.

sources.title: FCI: Labrador Retriever breed standard
sources.evidence: Kindly, biddable character with strong will to please; excellent nose, soft mouth and love of water; Newfoundland coastal history and early fame in British field trials.

VBO:0200919.summary: Mucuchies are known in Venezuela for loyalty, intelligence and a protective character, with their story closely tied to the Andean town that gave them their name. One dog, Nevado, holds a special place in national memory as Simón Bolívar’s companion. Cultural accounts of Nevado have helped make the breed a living symbol of Venezuelan history.
VBO:0200919.historicalRoots: Venezuelan Andean farm and livestock-guardian dog.

sources.title: Museo Bolivariano: Mucuchíes character and cultural history
sources.evidence: Museo Bolivariano/CNEH account identifies loyalty, intelligence, protection, Mucuchíes town origin and cultural association with Bolívar’s dog Nevado; story framed as national memory rather than every anecdote established fact.

VBO:0200934.summary: New Guinea Singing Dogs are remarkable communicators, producing wavering, musical howls. Their close wild relatives in the New Guinea highlands are shy and elusive, making field observation difficult. A 2020 genetic study linked those highland dogs with the captive singing-dog population, opening a new chapter in the conservation of this unusual canine lineage.
VBO:0200934.historicalRoots: New Guinea free-ranging dog lineage represented by both wild-associated and captive populations.

sources.title: UNSW: singing dogs and their wild highland relatives
sources.evidence: UNSW researchers describe distinctive howls, shy and reclusive highland wild dogs and the 2020 genetic connection to captive singing dogs; reserve explicitly scoped to wild population.

VBO:0200938.summary: Newfoundlands are known for a gentle, composed disposition, with a joyful side alongside their calmness. Their working history in Canada joins two demanding jobs: hauling heavy loads on land and helping people in the water, including rescue work. The breed’s reputation rests as much on that steady character and willingness to work as on its swimming ability.
VBO:0200938.historicalRoots: Canadian working water dog associated with Newfoundland fisheries and rescue work.

sources.title: FCI: Newfoundland breed standard
sources.evidence: FCI describes gentleness, serenity and joyful character; heavy-load sledge work and water/lifeguard roles in Newfoundland.

VBO:0201004.summary: Peruvian Hairless Dogs tend to be affectionate with their own people and more cautious around strangers, combining close companionship with an alert watchdog instinct. Their cultural history reaches far beyond the modern breed: depictions appear in the ceramics of several pre-Inca societies, including the Moche and Chancay.
VBO:0201004.interestingFact: Viringo is another name for the Peruvian Hairless Dog.
VBO:0201004.historicalRoots: Ancient Peruvian hairless-dog tradition documented in pre-Columbian art.

sources.title: FCI: Peruvian Hairless Dog breed standard
sources.evidence: Affectionate with familiar people, lively/alert and potentially wary with strangers; watchdog role; pre-Inca ceramics including Mochica and Chancay; name viringo.

VBO:0201102.summary: Pulis tend to be lively, quick-learning dogs with a watchful streak. Their Hungarian sheep-herding heritage is still central to their identity, and their readiness to learn has carried over into dog sports. The breed’s early history is traditionally linked to the livestock-keeping Magyars who migrated into the Carpathian Basin.
VBO:0201102.historicalRoots: Hungarian herding dog used around sheep.

sources.title: FCI: Puli breed standard
sources.evidence: Lively temperament, ability to learn, watchdog tendency and sporting use; Hungarian herding role; Magyar ancestry framed as probable in standard, rendered as traditional link.

VBO:0201135.summary: Rhodesian Ridgebacks tend to be composed and self-possessed, with a reserved approach to unfamiliar people. Their hunting history involved tracking game in small groups and keeping it at bay until a hunter arrived. The famous “lion dog” story refers to that demanding tracking and holding work, which relied on the dogs’ agility.
VBO:0201135.historicalRoots: Southern African multipurpose hound developed from imported and local ridged dogs.

sources.title: FCI: Rhodesian Ridgeback breed standard
sources.evidence: Dignified, intelligent, aloof with strangers; historical hunting in groups of two or three, tracking lions and keeping them at bay until the hunter arrived.

VBO:0201171.summary: Salukis tend to be independent and dignified, often greeting strangers with reserve. They come from a long Middle Eastern tradition of hunting by sight, with local dogs valued for pursuing the game found in their own region. In Middle Eastern tradition, Salukis were presented as marks of honor.
VBO:0201171.historicalRoots: Ancient Middle Eastern sighthound tradition spanning multiple regions and local types.

sources.title: FCI: Saluki breed standard
sources.evidence: Independent, intelligent, dignified and reserved temperament; long regional coursing tradition; local game specialization and presentation as gifts of honor.

VBO:0201220.summary: Shiba Inus are keenly alert and attentive to their surroundings, with a strong sense of attachment to familiar people. Their roots lie in hunting birds and small animals in Japan’s mountain country. When local strains became scarce after widespread crossing with imported hunting dogs, Japanese hunters helped organize the effort to preserve them.
VBO:0201220.historicalRoots: Japanese native hunting spitz associated with mountainous regions.

sources.title: FCI: Shiba Inu breed standard
sources.evidence: Faithful temperament, keen senses and high alertness; mountain hunting for birds/small game; decline through imported-dog crosses and hunter-led preservation beginning around 1928.

VBO:0201280.summary: Spanish Water Dogs tend to be lively, watchful and quick to grasp a task, with a strong willingness to work alongside people. Their traditional jobs ranged across herding, hunting and assisting fishermen. Readiness to learn and adapt to changing conditions was useful across that varied working life.
VBO:0201280.historicalRoots: Spanish multipurpose working dog used for herding and water-related tasks.

sources.title: FCI: Spanish Water Dog breed standard
sources.evidence: Lively, hardworking, watchful, faithful, obedient character and strong learning ability/adaptability; utilization as shepherd, hunter and fisherman’s assistant.

VBO:0201348.summary: Thai Ridgebacks are active, resilient dogs with a strong attachment to their families and a remarkable talent for jumping. In eastern Thailand they hunted, kept watch and accompanied carts on journeys. Difficult travel between communities helped preserve the local dogs, giving the breed a history tied to everyday work as well as companionship.
VBO:0201348.historicalRoots: Long-established Thai ridged dog associated with eastern regions of the country.

sources.title: FCI: Thai Ridgeback breed standard
sources.evidence: Tough, active, loyal family character and excellent jumping; eastern Thailand hunting, cart escort and watchdog roles; limited transport reducing crossbreeding.

VBO:0201421.summary: Whippets are often gentle, affectionate companions at home, with a very different intensity when something sets off their urge to chase. In northern England, working people developed them for small-game hunting and weekend racing. A favorite contest sent the dogs sprinting toward their owners, who waved a rag at the finish line.
VBO:0201421.interestingFact: Modern lure coursing gives Whippets an outlet for their pursuit instinct by sending them after an artificial lure.
VBO:0201421.historicalRoots: British sighthound developed for racing and small-game coursing.

sources.title: FCI: Whippet breed standard
sources.evidence: FCI describes gentle, affectionate, even disposition and adaptability to domestic and sporting life; hunting heritage.

sources.title: AKC: Whippet history and pursuit behavior
sources.evidence: AKC history documents home behavior and pursuit drive, northern English workers, small-game hunting, rag racing and modern lure coursing.

VBO:0201436.summary: Xoloitzcuintlis tend to be calm and fairly quiet, yet attentive to unfamiliar arrivals and sometimes reserved with strangers. Their companionship has deep roots in Mexican culture: in pre-Hispanic belief, these dogs were associated with Xolotl and guided the souls of the dead on their onward journey. The breed’s story combines everyday watchfulness with an extraordinary spiritual role.
VBO:0201436.historicalRoots: Ancient Mexican dog represented in pre-Columbian culture and modern hairless and coated forms.

sources.title: FCI: Xoloitzcuintli breed standard
sources.evidence: Calm, silent, cheerful and alert character, possible suspicion of strangers and watchdog/companion roles; association with Xolotl and guiding the dead in pre-Hispanic belief.
